howTo.name: Choose the milk and portion the trays
howTo.text: Any milk type is documented as suitable. Fill trays no more than three-quarters full; a secondary source puts roughly 3 to 4 cups of whole milk on a tray. Whole yields about 20 percent solids by volume, skim about 16 percent.

howTo.name: Pre-freeze
howTo.text: Pre-freeze milk at least 24 hours before loading, and up to 48 hours to shorten the freeze cycle. One manufacturer manual specifies pre-freezing on the trays in a deep freezer.

howTo.name: Run the cycle
howTo.text: The only general manufacturer figure for dairy is 13 to 35 hours; secondary sources report roughly 30 hours for a gallon on a large unit and 24 to 30 hours total batch. Machine size, load weight and tray depth all move this.

howTo.name: Check dryness before packaging
howTo.text: Break open pieces from the thickest areas of several trays and inspect the center for moisture, cold spots or softness; a dark middle indicates remaining moisture. A weight-stable reading across an extended dry cycle is the published alternative method.

howTo.name: Package to the storage conditions
howTo.text: Mylar with an oxygen absorber for long holds, sealed immediately after the dryness check; keep cool, dry, dark and below 85 degrees Fahrenheit. Jars are the published option for stock you open often.

howTo.name: Rehydrate
howTo.text: One part powder to one part water per the manufacturer; a secondary source specifies 1 to 1 and a third cups of powder per quart jar, cold water, shaken about 30 seconds.

faq.question: Does the fat in whole milk make it a bad freeze-drying candidate?
faq.answer: No source says so. Fat does not sublimate, and every tier agrees higher fat means shorter storage life and higher rancidity risk. But no manufacturer, extension service or peer-reviewed source publishes a fat percentage above which a food fails, and none applies a fat objection to fluid milk. Skim will keep longer than whole by that same logic, though no source publishes the two side by side.

faq.question: Can you freeze-dry raw milk?
faq.answer: Utah State University Extension classifies raw milk and raw dairy as high-risk and answers no without pasteurization, because unpasteurized dairy can harbor Listeria, Salmonella or E. coli. Freeze-drying does not pasteurize and does not kill bacteria; it preserves them dormant, and adding water back is the step that reactivates them. No manufacturer addresses raw milk as a distinct product.

faq.question: How much powder does a gallon of milk make?
faq.answer: A secondary source reports about 5 cups of powder from a gallon of whole milk, roughly 20 percent, and about 4 cups from skim, roughly 16 percent. No extension service publishes a yield figure for any food, so treat it as the only published figure rather than a verified one.

faq.question: How long does freeze-dried milk keep?
faq.answer: There is no settled answer and we do not publish a guarantee. Manufacturers claim up to 25 years in mylar with an oxygen absorber under ideal conditions; UC ANR states that claim has not been corroborated by university studies for home freeze dryers and does not recommend consumption beyond 5 to 10 years; Utah State Extension says no real data exists on home freeze-dried shelf life. A secondary milk-specific figure is 10 or more years in mylar and about a year in jars.

faq.question: How do you know the milk is actually dry?
faq.answer: The tray can read dry on the surface while the center is not. Harvest Right's published check is to break open the thickest pieces from several trays and look for moisture, cold spots, softness or darker color; University of Minnesota Extension looks for dark spots at the center. Stay Fresh publishes the only weight-based method found: weigh the trays at cycle completion and again after extended drying, and a weight that stops changing indicates adequate dryness.

bodyHtml:
The short version: Whole milk freeze-dries and rehydrates well, and the fat myth — that milk's fat makes it a poor candidate — is half right for the wrong reason. Every source agrees fat does not sublimate and shortens storage life [11][12][17][1], but no source at any tier publishes a fat percentage above which a food fails, and whole milk is the one dairy product with published yield and rehydration numbers behind it [22]. Pasteurized milk is routine; raw milk is where the process stops being a preservation question and becomes a pathogen question [1][18].

The fat question, sourced

Start with the mechanism, because it is the one point on which manufacturers and extension services do not disagree. Harvest Right states it plainly: “Freeze drying removes water, but oil remains” [11]. Stay Fresh's owner's manual says the same thing from the failure side: “the process only removes water from the food and the oil may go rancid after packaging” [17]. Sublimation is a water-removal process. Whatever fat went onto the tray comes off the tray.

What that means for milk is a storage-life effect, not a suitability verdict. Here is what each tier actually publishes about fat, in its own words.

SourcePublished statement on fatWhat it does not say
Harvest Right [11]“Freeze drying removes water, but oil remains”; foods that are nearly pure fat do not freeze dry well on their ownDoes not name milk as a high-fat exclusion; does not give a fat percentage
Harvest Right [12]“Foods that contain higher amounts of fat generally have shorter storage lives”Does not quantify how much shorter, for any food
Utah State University Extension [1]High fat content increases the risk of rancidity during storage; for high-fat cheeses, melt or blend and spread thinlyDoes not apply a fat objection to fluid milk
University of Minnesota Extension [3]Home freeze-drying works well for proteins, but not for foods that are high in fatDoes not define “high in fat” numerically or place milk on either side
Stay Fresh [17]Water is removed; “the oil may go rancid after packaging”Does not give a fat ceiling or a revised shelf-life figure

The gap in the right-hand column is the finding. Searches across manufacturer, extension and peer-reviewed tiers turned up no numeric fat threshold for any food — no percentage above which a source says stop. Every fat caution in this category is qualitative. So “milk is too fatty to freeze-dry” has no published threshold behind it, and neither would a claim that whole milk is fine forever.

Two things follow that are worth holding together. First, fat direction-of-travel is well documented: more fat, shorter storage life, higher rancidity risk [12][1][17]. Skim will therefore keep longer than whole, though no source publishes the two side by side. Second, the oldest source in this pack found a fat effect in the finished powder rather than in the cycle: the Journal of Dairy Science in 1952 reported that “the fat emulsion of freeze-dried powder is partially destabilized” and that freeze-dried milk “frequently acquires a fruity flavor” [20]. That study concluded freeze-drying did not produce a more satisfactory product than spray-drying at the scale and process of its era — a 74-year-old research-scale finding, squarely opposed to how milk is framed in manufacturer marketing today [8][20]. We record both; neither has been reconciled by anything published since.

Dairy vs raw, what regulators say

The safety claim that governs this entire section is one line, repeated by every extension service in the pack: “Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria. Instead, it preserves microorganisms in a dormant state,” per Jose Brandao of Utah State University Extension [2]. University of Maine Extension states it the same way: freeze drying does not destroy harmful bacteria that can cause foodborne illness [4]. The dormancy ends when water goes back in [1].

Pasteurized milk. Treated as a suitable candidate across extension and manufacturer sources alike [1][5][8][10]. The pasteurization step already happened; the freeze dryer is doing preservation work on an already-treated product.

Raw milk. Utah State University Extension classifies raw milk, raw cheese and raw dairy as high-risk and answers “no” without pasteurization, on the grounds that unpasteurized dairy can harbor Listeria, Salmonella or E. coli [1]. No manufacturer in the pack addresses raw milk as a distinct product at all. A secondary source states the obvious corollary directly: the process does not pasteurize raw milk [22].

Now the regulators, and here the finding is mostly an absence. FDA's raw milk page documents the pathogen risk and the role of pasteurization in largely eliminating it — and mentions freeze-drying nowhere [18]. The Association of Food and Drug Officials' state-by-state raw milk guidance does not address freeze-drying, dehydrating or powdering as a processing category either [19]. That is a description of what the published record contains, not advice about what anyone may lawfully sell; whether drying raw milk changes its regulatory status in a given state is not answered by any source we could retrieve.

The peer-reviewed record on powder gives the durability question some shape without settling it for home equipment. Salmonella survived three months in skim milk powder at a water activity of 0.33, and E. coli O157:H7 survived a year in infant formula powder held at 5°C [21]. Those products were powdered, not confirmed freeze-dried, and none of it is a home-unit study — but dry does not mean dead, and that is the point the extension sources make in plainer words [1][2][4].

Preparation and loading

Milk is a liquid load, so the constraints are tray depth, pre-freezing and containment rather than slicing. Here are the published figures, with tiers marked, because most of the granular milk numbers come from a secondary source rather than a manufacturer.

ItemPublished figureSource and tier
Milk typeAny milk type; whole retains more solids than skimHarvest Right [10]; yield split from a secondary source [22]
Tray fillFill trays no more than three-quarters fullHarvest Right, manufacturer [10]
Volume per tray~3–4 cups whole milk per traySecondary [22]
Pre-freezeAt least 24 hours for milk, eggs, soups and stews; up to 48 hours to shorten the freeze cycleHarvest Right [10][15]; Stay Fresh manual specifies pre-freezing on the trays in a deep freezer [17]
Cycle time13–35 hours is the only general manufacturer figure for meats, meals and dairy; ~30 hours for one gallon on a large unit; 24–30 hours total batchHarvest Right FAQ [15]; secondary [22][23]
YieldWhole ~20% (1 gal → ~5 cups powder); skim ~16% (1 gal → ~4 cups)Secondary [22] — no extension service publishes a yield figure for any food

Treat any single hour figure as conditional. None of the sources control for machine size, load weight, tray depth or starting temperature, so the same gallon on two machines is not the same cycle.

The endpoint matters more than the clock, and milk is exactly the load where the clock lies. Harvest Right's caution is worth quoting because it applies hardest to a poured liquid that dries into a slab: “The outside of a piece of food can feel completely dry even when moisture remains in the center” [14]. Their published check is to break pieces open and inspect the center for moisture, cold spots or softness, testing the thickest pieces from several trays [14]. University of Minnesota Extension's version is to cut pieces in half and look for dark spots in the middle [3]. Stay Fresh publishes the only weight-based method found: weigh each tray at cycle completion and again after extended drying, and “if the weight remains consistent, this indicates that the food is adequately dry,” working to a scale error of about one gram [16]. Harvest Right publishes no weight method on any page checked [14].

Rehydration

Milk is one of the few foods in this category with a published reconstitution ratio rather than a technique. Harvest Right gives 1:1 powder to water [8]. A secondary source is more specific: 1 to 1⅓ cups of powder (roughly 75–100 g) per quart jar, cold water, shaken about 30 seconds [22]. For other dairy, Harvest Right's own guidance is technique rather than ratio — add water gradually and stir until the product returns to its original state [9].

Two practical notes that fall out of the sourced record. Cold water and a hard shake exist in the secondary instruction for a reason that no source explains in mechanism terms, so we present it as published practice rather than as chemistry. And rehydrated milk is a fresh dairy product again: the dormancy point from the safety sources cuts both ways, since adding water is the step that reactivates anything the drying preserved [1][2].

Storage with conditions

The 25-year number is the most contested claim in this category, and milk sits inside that dispute rather than outside it.

PositionPublished statementAttached conditions
Harvest Right [12][13]Many properly packaged freeze-dried foods can last up to 25 years or longer under ideal conditionsMylar plus oxygen absorber; cool, low humidity, minimal light, stable environment, below 85°F; explicitly conditioned on fat content
Secondary, milk-specific [22]10+ years in mylar with an oxygen absorber; about a year or less in mason jarsNot a manufacturer or extension figure
Utah State University Extension [1]Freeze-dried foods can remain safe and stable for 10–15 years, sometimes up to 25Airtight, moisture-proof packaging
UC ANR [5]The 25-year claim “has not been corroborated by university studies for home freeze dryers”; consumption is not recommended beyond 5–10 years after processingApplies to home-produced product specifically
Utah State University Extension [6]“No real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products”; anchors instead to an 8–10 year conservative estimate for commercially produced metal-mylar productNotes the first home unit went on sale in 2013
Iowa State University Extension [7]“There is no verification that food will last 25 years at this point”None given

We do not publish a shelf-life guarantee for freeze-dried milk, and nothing above supports one. What the record does support is a set of conditions that every source agrees on: mylar with an oxygen absorber for anything meant to sit for years, kept cool, dry, dark and below 85°F [12][13]; jars for what you will open often, at a much shorter horizon [12][22]. Fat pulls the number down rather than up, which is the one place the fat question rejoins storage: skim keeps longer than whole, by every source's logic, though none publishes the pair [12][1].

  • Long-hold portions: mylar, oxygen absorber, sealed immediately after the dryness check [13][14].
  • Working stock: a jar you open weekly, understanding that every opening admits moisture and oxygen [12].
  • Whole vs skim: if the batch is going into deep storage, the lower-fat product is the one the sources point at [12][1].
  • Packaging: our Freeze-Drying Packaging Starter Kit (100 mylar bags in three sizes, 100 absorbers, labels) covers the mylar-and-absorber path above. Sold by Sublime Pantry.

Moisture removal itself has four published figures and no reconciliation: about 97% [5], roughly 90% by sublimation plus 1–2% by desorption [3], up to 98% [4], and 98–99% for product a manufacturer describes as intended to last 25 years or more [16]. Every one is framed as percent removed. No source publishes a residual-moisture target to dry to.

What we could not source

  • No fat percentage threshold, anywhere. No source at any tier — manufacturer, extension or peer-reviewed — publishes a numeric fat ceiling for any food. The lean preference is qualitative only, which means the common “too fatty to freeze-dry” framing has no published line behind it.
  • No pathogen-survival study on freeze-dried raw milk specifically. The closest available work is on powdered milk generally [21].
  • No regulator position on freeze-drying as a processing category for raw milk. FDA's raw milk page and AFDO's state-by-state guidance both omit freeze-drying, dehydrating and powdering entirely [18][19].
  • Fresh-to-dried yield is essentially unpublished. Milk is one of only two foods in the whole pack with any yield figure at all, and the milk figure is secondary [22]. No extension service publishes a yield percentage for any food.
  • No residual-moisture-remaining target. All four published moisture figures describe percent removed, never percent remaining [3][4][5][16].
  • No manufacturer weight-based dryness method. The weight-stable endpoint is Stay Fresh's [16]; Harvest Right publishes only the break test and a moisture meter [14].
  • The National Center for Home Food Preservation has no freeze-drying publication. The highest-authority home-preservation body in the United States has nothing public on home freeze dryers, which is why every extension citation here comes from a state service instead.
  • No comparison of whole vs skim storage life. The direction is documented; the pair is never published together.
  • No source explains why cold water and a 30-second shake. The instruction exists [22]; the mechanism does not.

Sublime Pantry has not bench-tested any freeze dryer or any food. Everything above is what the published record says, with the gaps marked as gaps.
